subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Stages of Development and Developmental Tasks
Memory, Transfer of Learning and Complex Thinking

subjective.question: Define growth and development.
subjective.answer: Growth: The term growth denotes a net increase in the size or mass of the tissue. It is largely attributed to multiplication of cells and increase in the intracellular substance. According to Hurlock, growth is change in size, in proportion, disappearance of old features and acquisition of new ones. According to Crow and Crow (1962), growth refers to structural and physiological changes. Development: Development specifies maturation of functions. It is related to the maturation and myelination of the nervous system and indicates acquisition of a variety of skills for optimal functioning of the individual. According to Hurlock (1959), development means a progressive series of changes that occur in an orderly, predictable pattern as a result of maturation and experience. According to Liebert, Poulos and Marmor (1979), development refers to a process of change in growth and capability over time, as a function of both maturation and interaction with the environment.

subjective.question: Describe any two factors that affect human development.
subjective.answer: 1. Sex: Sex is a very important factor which influences human growth and development. There is a lot of difference in growth and development between girls and boys. Physical growth of girls in their teens is faster than boys. Overall, the body structure and growth of girls are different from boys. 2. Socioeconomic factors: Socioeconomic factors definitely have some effect. It has been seen that children from different socioeconomic levels vary in average body size at all ages, the upper level families being always more advanced. The most important reasons behind this are better nutrition, better facilities, regular meals, sleep and exercise. (Other factors include race and pollution: air and indoor pollution can result in ill health, which negatively impacts human growth and development.)

subjective.question: What are the aspects of human development? Explain briefly.
subjective.answer: There are four aspects of human development discussed in this course: 1. Physical Development: It deals with changes in body structure and functions, mainly due to growth or maturation. Learning plays little role in physical development. 2. Social Development: It refers to changes in the way an individual relates to others. A large part of these changes is due to learning. 3. Emotional Development: It means changes in the way an individual becomes capable of understanding, expressing and controlling personal feelings, understanding the feelings of others and responding to them. In emotional development, maturation and learning both play an important role. 4. Intellectual Development: It refers to changes by which mental processes become more complex and sophisticated. It is influenced by both heredity (maturation) and environment (learning).

subjective.question: Elucidate the role of maturation in intellectual development of a child.
subjective.answer: Maturation is the unfolding or ripening of abilities, characteristics, traits and potentialities present at birth; it is an inner growth process unaffected by training. In intellectual development, maturation of the nervous system — including myelination of nerve fibres — sets the readiness for mental processes to become more complex and sophisticated. A child can learn a mental skill only when the underlying structures have matured; for example, abstract reasoning appears only after the brain structures supporting it have matured. Intellectual development is therefore under the influence of both heredity (maturation) and environment (learning): maturation provides the biological readiness and sequence, while learning and experience determine how fully the matured capacities are used.

subjective.topic: Stages of Development and Developmental Tasks
subjective.question: Write down the stages of development.
subjective.answer: The developmental stages are: • Infancy – Early Childhood (birth to 5 years) • Middle Childhood (6 to 12 years) • Adolescence (13 to 18 years) • Early Adulthood (19 to 29 years) • Middle Adulthood (30–60 years) • Later Maturity (above 60 years)

subjective.topic: Stages of Development and Developmental Tasks
subjective.question: What is developmental task theory? Who elaborated it?
subjective.answer: Although many theorists contributed to the Developmental Tasks Theory, it was Robert J. Havighurst who elaborated this theory in a most systematic and extensive manner. Havighurst's main claim is that development is continuous throughout the entire lifespan, occurring in stages, where the individual moves from one stage to the next by means of successful resolution of problems or performance of developmental tasks. Havighurst identified three sources of developmental tasks, and the theory covers six stages of life.

subjective.topic: Stages of Development and Developmental Tasks
subjective.question: Explain the developmental tasks of Infancy and Early Childhood (birth to 5 years).
subjective.answer: The developmental tasks of Infancy – Early Childhood (birth to 5 years) are: • Learning to take solid foods • Learning to walk • Learning to talk • Learning to control the elimination of body wastes • Learning gender differences • Forming concepts and learning language to describe social and physical reality • Getting ready to read

subjective.topic: Stages of Development and Developmental Tasks
subjective.question: What are the characteristics of preschool and kindergarten children?
subjective.answer: Preschool and kindergarten (3–6 years) is the stage where children have their first exposure to the school routine and interact with more than a few peers. They get opportunities to prepare for initial academic experiences in group settings. It is important for them to learn to follow directions and get along with others. Preschool children are very active: they have good control of their bodies and enjoy activity for its own sake. Their large muscles are more developed than their small muscles, so gross motor skills (running, jumping, climbing, hopping) improve greatly, while fine motor control of fingers and hands is still developing.

subjective.topic: Stages of Development and Developmental Tasks
subjective.question: Define primary grades and describe the children of this stage.
subjective.answer: Primary grades are grades 1, 2 and 3 (6–9 years). This age is the age of first experiences with school learning. Children are eager to learn reading and writing and are likely to be upset due to lack of progress in academics. They learn initial attitudes toward schooling, and initial roles in a group setting are formed. At this stage teachers should use visual aids and concrete examples during teaching and avoid teaching metaphors, idioms and proverbs.

subjective.topic: Stages of Development and Developmental Tasks
subjective.question: How should a teacher behave with preschool and kindergarten children?
subjective.answer: Teachers should allow children to settle their differences themselves and intervene only when a quarrel gets out of hand. They may either suggest another equally attractive activity or impose rules to take turns. Teachers should encourage desirable forms of dramatic play and decide on their own what restrictions should be imposed in order to discourage aggressive behaviour. Because preschool children are very active, teachers should provide many opportunities to run, climb and jump, followed by quiet activities and frequent rest periods.

subjective.topic: Stages of Development and Developmental Tasks
subjective.question: Write a note on the social interaction of preschool children.
subjective.answer: Social interaction is an essential part of social development during the preschool years. Preschool is the child's first exposure to a social world beyond the family, where he interacts with many peers in group settings. Through structured play and group activities, children learn to follow directions, take turns, share, and get along with others. The study of the social interaction experienced by pairs of preschool-age children during a structured play situation provides useful information about the development of social behaviour, because it is through such interaction that the foundations of social development — relating to others, cooperation and control of behaviour — are laid.

subjective.question: Explain Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences.
subjective.answer: Howard Gardner proposed that there is not one intelligence but multiple intelligences: 1. Logical-Mathematical Intelligence: solving mathematical and logic problems; ability to make and read graphs; organization of things. 2. Verbal-Linguistic Intelligence: people high in it are good at poems, rhyming words, reading and writing, and storytelling. 3. Interpersonal Intelligence: understanding other people's emotions and the social etiquettes and norms of different situations; such people can be good leaders or managers who coordinate with employees. 4. Bodily-Kinesthetic Intelligence: ability to use the body purposefully; dancers, actors, soldiers and sports athletes excel in it. 5. Musical Intelligence: associated with rhythmic and harmonic music; being able to interpret sounds, rhythms, tones and pitches, and to compose or play an instrument. 6. Visual-Spatial Intelligence: how well you visualize something in your mind's eye — e.g., getting through a maze or reading a map. 7. Intrapersonal Intelligence: how you understand yourself — self-awareness, control of emotions and moods, and knowledge of your strengths and weaknesses. 8. Naturalistic Intelligence: recognizing and classifying all types of animals, plants and minerals in the real world; hunters, fishermen, chefs and botanists are strong in it.

subjective.question: Explain the meanings/definitions of intelligence given by different psychologists.
subjective.answer: • Intelligence is an inferred process that humans use to explain the different degrees of adaptive success in people's behaviour. • It is the mental ability that enables one to adapt to, shape, or select one's environment. • It is the ability to judge, comprehend and reason. • It is the ability to understand and deal with people, objects and symbols. • David Wechsler defined it as the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally and to deal effectively with his environment. • In all cultures, intelligence is the ability to learn from experience, solve problems, and use our knowledge to adapt to new situations.

subjective.question: Define verbal-linguistic intelligence by giving one example.
subjective.answer: Verbal-linguistic intelligence is the capacity to use language effectively. People with high verbal-linguistic intelligence are good at poems, rhyming words, reading and writing, and storytelling. Example: a poet or a storyteller shows high verbal-linguistic intelligence.

subjective.question: List the personality assessment techniques and explain the physiological (physical test) methods.
subjective.answer: Personality assessment techniques are: (1) Subjective Methods, (2) Objective Methods, (3) Projective Methods (e.g., the Rorschach Ink Blot Test and the Thematic Apperception Test), (4) Psycho-Analytical Methods, and (5) Physical Test Methods or Physiological Methods. In the physiological methods of personality assessment, the following instruments are commonly used: 1. Pneumograph: used for measuring the rate of respiratory activity of the individual. 2. Plethysmograph: used for measuring the individual's blood pressure. 3. Sphygmograph: used for measuring the activity of the heart. 4. Electrocardiograph: used for measuring the activity of the heart. 5. Electro-encephalograph: used for measuring the electrical activity in the human brain. 6. Graphology: the individual's personality is assessed through a study of his handwriting. 7. Electromyogram: used for measuring muscular activity.

subjective.question: Describe any one level of Kohlberg's moral development.
subjective.answer: Level 1: Preconventional Morality (0–9 years). This level consists of two stages: Stage 1 – Obedience and Punishment: Especially common in young children, though adults are also capable of expressing this type of reasoning. At this stage, children see rules as fixed and absolute. The child obeys rules in order to avoid punishment, determines right and wrong by what is punished and what is not punished, obeys superior authority and allows that authority to make the rules, and is responsive to rules that affect his/her physical well-being. Stage 2 – Individualism and Exchange (naively egoistic orientation): children judge actions by whether they serve individual needs and satisfy their own interests.

subjective.question: What is moral development?
subjective.answer: Moral development is the gradual development of an individual's concept of right or wrong — conscience, religious values, social attitudes and certain behaviour.

subjective.question: Explain Gilligan's theory of moral development.
subjective.answer: Carol Gilligan, a student of Lawrence Kohlberg, proposed that morality in girls develops through three stages, based on the ethic of care rather than only justice and fairness: 1. Selfish Stage (Orientation to Individual Survival): the girl/woman is concerned only with her own survival and what is practical and best for her. 2. Belief in Conventional Morality (Goodness as Self-Sacrifice): she believes in conventional morality — goodness means caring for and sacrificing for others, and she gives up her own wishes for the sake of others. 3. Post-Conventional Stage (Morality of Non-Violence): she arrives at a morality of care and non-violence, balancing care for herself with care for others, and makes decisions on the principle of not hurting anyone, including herself. A major criticism of Gilligan's theory is that she collected her data from females only.

subjective.question: Write the eight stages of Erikson's psychosocial theory with their age groups.
subjective.answer: Erikson's psychosocial theory divides personality development into eight stages, each with a crisis to be resolved: 1. Trust vs. Mistrust (birth to 1 year) 2. Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt (18 months to 3 years) 3. Initiative vs. Guilt (3 to 5 years) 4. Industry vs. Inferiority (5 to 13 years) 5. Identity vs. Role Confusion (13 to 21 years) 6. Intimacy vs. Isolation (21 to 39 years) 7. Generativity vs. Stagnation (40 to 65 years) 8. Ego Integrity vs. Despair (65 years and above) At each stage the person must cope with the crisis adaptively or maladaptively: responding adaptively means acquiring the strengths needed for the next stage, while a maladaptive response makes it less likely that the person will be able to adapt to later problems.

subjective.question: Explain any two stages of Piaget's cognitive development.
subjective.answer: 1. Sensorimotor Stage (birth to 2 years): The infant learns about the world through senses and motor actions. The major achievement is object permanence — knowing that objects continue to exist even when they cannot be seen. 2. Preoperational Stage (2 to 7 years): Children begin to think symbolically and learn to use words and pictures to represent objects. They tend to be egocentric and struggle to see things from the perspective of others, and their thinking is not yet logical. (The other two stages are the Concrete Operational Stage, 7–11 years, in which children begin to think logically about concrete events, and the Formal Operational Stage, 12 years and above, in which the ability to think about abstract ideas and situations develops.)

subjective.question: How do schemas work in Piaget's theory?
subjective.answer: A schema includes both a category of knowledge and the process of obtaining that knowledge; it is the mental framework a child uses to organize and interpret experience. Schemas work through adaptation, which has two processes: assimilation — interpreting new experiences in terms of existing schemas — and accommodation — changing or altering existing schemas in the light of new information and experiences. Piaget believed that all children try to strike a balance (equilibration) between assimilation and accommodation, and in this way their cognitive structures develop through interaction with the environment.

subjective.question: What is learning? Give definitions.
subjective.answer: "A persisting change in human performance or performance potential… (brought) about as a result of the learner's interaction with the environment" (Driscoll, 1994). "The relatively permanent change in a person's knowledge or behaviour due to experience" (Mayer, 1982). There are three main theories of how people learn: Behaviourism, Social Learning Theory and Cognitivism.

subjective.question: What is classical conditioning?
subjective.answer: Classical conditioning is a behaviourist learning theory in which individuals learn by association, pairing automatic responses to new stimuli. It involves the simultaneous presentation of two events: a stimulus is presented in order to get a response. It was introduced by Ivan Pavlov through his experiments with dogs, in which the dogs learned to salivate at the sound of a bell that had been paired with food.

subjective.question: What is meant by operant conditioning?
subjective.answer: Operant conditioning is a type of learning, introduced by B.F. Skinner, in which a behaviour is strengthened (meaning it will occur more frequently) when it is followed by reinforcement, and weakened (will happen less frequently) when followed by punishment. Operant conditioning is based on this simple idea of consequences controlling behaviour.

subjective.question: Write a note on the background of Vygotsky.
subjective.answer: Lev Semyonovich Vygotsky was called "The Mozart of Psychology". He was born in 1896 — the same year as Piaget — in the small Russian town of Orsha, and belonged to a middle-class Jewish family. He entered Moscow University through a lottery in 1913 and graduated in December 1917 with a degree in law. He completed 270 scientific articles, numerous lectures and ten books based on a wide range of Marxist-based psychological and teaching theories. He died on June 10, 1934, at the young age of thirty-seven, after a long battle with TB. Vygotsky's work did not become known in the West until 1958 and was not published there until 1962.

subjective.question: Define Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD).
subjective.answer: Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) is the difference between what a child can do independently and what the child needs help from a more knowledgeable person to do. Closely related to it is scaffolding — the role of teachers and others in supporting the learner's development and providing support structures to get to the next stage or level.

subjective.question: According to Vygotsky, "learning appears twice". Explain.
subjective.answer: According to Vygotsky, every function in the child's cultural development appears twice: first on the social level, and later on the individual level; first between people (interpsychological), and then inside the child (intrapsychological). In other words, learning first takes place through interaction with others and is later internalized by the child.

subjective.question: Explain the main principles and concepts of the sociocultural theory of Vygotsky.
subjective.answer: The main principles and concepts of Vygotsky's sociocultural theory are: • Children construct their knowledge. Knowledge is not transferred passively, but is personally constructed. • Learning is mediated. Cognitive development is not a direct result of activity, but is indirect; other people must interact with the learner and use mediatory tools to facilitate the learning process, and then cognitive development may occur. • Language plays a central role in mental development. The most significant sociocultural tool is language, as it is used to teach tool use and is vital in the process of developing higher psychological functions. • Development proceeds through dyadic interactions — e.g., a child being taught by a parent how to perform some culturally specific action — rather than by the child alone.

subjective.question: Define dyadic interaction.
subjective.answer: Dyadic interaction means focusing on interactions within a pair (dyad) — for example, a child being taught by a parent how to perform some culturally specific action — rather than on the child by himself. In Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, such social interaction is the basis of learning and cognitive development.

subjective.question: Where can Vygotsky's theory be applied?
subjective.answer: Vygotsky's sociocultural theory has direct relevance and implications in the classroom, especially the second language classroom. Because learning is socially mediated and language is the central tool of mental development, teachers should organize collaborative learning, use dialogue and discussion, provide scaffolding within each learner's Zone of Proximal Development, and gradually withdraw support as the learner becomes independent.

subjective.topic: Memory, Transfer of Learning and Complex Thinking
subjective.question: Define trace decay theory of forgetting.
subjective.answer: Trace decay theory suggests that information stored in memory fades away (decays) with the passage of time if it is not used or rehearsed. According to this theory, Short Term Memory can only hold information for between 15 and 30 seconds; forgetting from short term memory is explained by trace decay and displacement. The memory trace simply weakens and disappears when it is not refreshed.

subjective.topic: Memory, Transfer of Learning and Complex Thinking
subjective.question: What is forgetting? Explain the main theories of forgetting.
subjective.answer: Forgetting is the inability to retrieve previously stored information. Its main theories are: 1. Trace Decay Theory: memory traces decay with time; it explains forgetting from short term memory (along with displacement). 2. Interference Theory: new and old learning interfere with each other — retroactive interference (new learning disturbs old) and proactive interference (old learning disturbs new). It explains forgetting from long term memory. 3. Lack of Association: when new information is not related and tied with previously learnt, relevant ideas, it remains floating in memory without proper anchors (cues or signals) and is forgotten. 4. Retrieval Failure Theory (cue-dependent forgetting): we forget because we are not able to use the correct cues to retrieve or access the information. 5. Motivated Forgetting: based on Freud's theory, forgetting works as a defence mechanism in which people are motivated to forget unwanted or disturbing memories, consciously (suppression) or unconsciously (repression).

subjective.topic: Memory, Transfer of Learning and Complex Thinking
subjective.question: What is transfer of learning? Explain its types.
subjective.answer: Transfer of learning is the process in which something previously learnt influences current learning. Its main types are: 1. Positive transfer: previous learning helps subsequent learning. 2. Negative transfer: prior learning interferes with subsequent learning. 3. Zero transfer: previous learning has no effect on subsequent learning. Positive transfer is further divided into: Specific transfer — due to specific similarities between the two tasks (e.g., similarities between French and Spanish in vocabulary and sentence structure); General transfer — due to the use of learning strategies such as elaboration, imagery and cues; Vertical transfer — previously learnt capability helps in learning more complex material in the same area; and Lateral transfer — previously learnt capability is used in solving a similar problem in a different context. Thorndike and Woodworth developed an alternative behavioural explanation of how transfer of learning occurs (the theory of identical elements).

subjective.topic: Memory, Transfer of Learning and Complex Thinking
subjective.question: What is metacognition? Write a note on complex thinking.
subjective.answer: Metacognition means "thinking about thinking": it refers to higher order thinking which involves active control over the cognitive processes engaged in learning. Facilitating complex thinking includes developing critical thinking (analysing the reliability and validity of information), creative thinking (making or doing something new that is also useful or valued by others — stimulated by open-ended questions, which produce divergent thinking), and problem solving (analysing a complex and ambiguous situation and finding a solution). Teachers can promote complex thinking through strategies such as concept maps — graphic depictions of relationships among a set of concepts, terms or ideas — outlining, summarizing and self-questioning.
